    {
      "cell_type": "markdown",
      "id": "9d071693",
      "metadata": {
        "id": "9d071693"
      },
      "source": [
        "\n",
        "**Discussion of trade-offs.** Both mitigation strategies substantially reduce the share of recommendations drawn from already-popular products and increase catalogue coverage relative to the baseline, confirming the popularity bias identified in Section 18 is **addressable**, not fixed. However, neither mitigation is \"free\":\n",
        "\n",
        "* **Mitigation 1 (continuous popularity penalty)** achieves the strongest, most tunable de-biasing (via α) but at the largest cost to Precision@K/NDCG@K — because it rescales *every* candidate's score by its popularity, including cases where a popular item genuinely was the most relevant choice for that customer.\n",
        "* **Mitigation 2 (long-tail quota)** achieves meaningfully improved diversity/coverage while **retaining more of the baseline's accuracy**, because it only forces long-tail *exposure* in a bounded number of slots rather than distorting every score — but its de-biasing strength is capped by the chosen quota, and forcing weak/irrelevant long-tail items into a list can itself hurt user trust if not tuned carefully.\n",
        "\n",
        "In practice, a production system might combine a **mild** popularity penalty (small α) with a **modest** long-tail quota, and tune both against business metrics (e.g. long-run customer retention, seller equity) rather than offline Precision@K alone — offline accuracy is not the only, or even the primary, objective once fairness and ecosystem health are considered.\n"
      ]
    },
    {
      "cell_type": "markdown",
      "id": "bd4856bd",
      "metadata": {
        "id": "bd4856bd"
      },
      "source": [
        "\n",
        "## 22. Generative AI in the Ethical Context\n",
        "\n",
        "**Where Generative AI could sit in RetailRecX.** A natural extension is a **post-hoc explanation-generation layer**: the existing pipeline (recommendation engine → selected products → SHAP/LIME feature attributions) feeds its structured output into an LLM, which converts feature attributions into a fluent, natural-language explanation for the end user (e.g. turning `prod_num_customers > 118` and `had_prior_interaction = 1` into *\"We recommended this because you've bought similar items before, and it's popular with shoppers like you.\"*). A further extension is a **conversational recommendation interface**, where a user can ask follow-up questions (\"why not show me something cheaper?\") and the system adjusts recommendations and explanations interactively.\n",
        "\n",
        "To illustrate the *mechanism* concretely (without depending on an external LLM API call, which is out of scope for this notebook), the cell below implements a small **rule-based natural-language template** that converts the top SHAP contributions for an instance into a plain-English explanation — a deliberately simple stand-in for what a full generative model would produce more fluently, but useful for grounding the discussion that follows.\n"
      ]
    },
    {
      "cell_type": "code",
      "execution_count": 45,
      "id": "006660d4",
      "metadata": {
        "execution": {
          "iopub.execute_input": "2026-08-12T17:29:11.677080Z",
          "iopub.status.busy": "2026-08-12T17:29:11.676526Z",
          "iopub.status.idle": "2026-08-12T17:29:11.683486Z",
          "shell.execute_reply": "2026-08-12T17:29:11.682762Z"
        },
        "colab": {
          "base_uri": "https://localhost:8080/"
        },
        "id": "006660d4",
        "outputId": "4cafccb8-5946-4ab5-bcae-df70feadf653"
      },
      "outputs": [
        {
          "output_type": "stream",
          "name": "stdout",
          "text": [
            "Rule-based (non-generative) natural-language explanation for CustomerID 12347, product 22727:\n",
            "\n",
            "We recommended this product because you purchased this product relatively recently, and you have purchased this product multiple times before.\n"
          ]
        }
      ],
      "source": [
        "FEATURE_EXPLANATIONS = {\n",
        "    'had_prior_interaction': \"you have purchased this exact product before\",\n",
        "    'cp_purchase_count': \"you have purchased this product multiple times before\",\n",
        "    'cp_recency_days': \"you purchased this product relatively recently\",\n",
        "    'prod_total_qty': \"this product is one of our best-selling items\",\n",
        "    'prod_num_customers': \"many other customers have also purchased this product\",\n",
        "    'prod_popularity_rank': \"this product ranks highly in overall popularity\",\n",
        "    'cust_total_spend': \"you are a high-value customer with substantial historical spend\",\n",
        "    'cust_avg_basket_size': \"you tend to purchase in larger quantities\",\n",
        "    'cust_unique_products': \"you have a history of buying a wide variety of products\",\n",
        "    'prod_avg_price': \"this product's price fits your typical purchase pattern\",\n",
        "    'cust_country_enc': \"this product is popular in your region\",\n",
        "}\n",
        "def generate_rule_based_explanation(shap_values_for_instance, feature_names, top_n=3):\n",
        "    contributions = pd.Series(shap_values_for_instance, index=feature_names).sort_values(key=abs, ascending=False)\n",
        "    reasons = []\n",
        "    for feat, val in contributions.head(top_n).items():\n",
        "        if val > 0 and feat in FEATURE_EXPLANATIONS:\n",
        "            reasons.append(FEATURE_EXPLANATIONS[feat])\n",
        "    if not reasons:\n",
        "        return \"This product was recommended based on your overall purchase profile.\"\n",
        "    return \"We recommended this product because \" + \", and \".join(reasons) + \".\"\n",
        "\n",
        "template_explanation = generate_rule_based_explanation(single_explanation.values, FEATURE_COLS)\n",
        "print(f\"Rule-based (non-generative) natural-language explanation for CustomerID {example_cust}, \"\n",
        "      f\"product {top_rec['StockCode']}:\\n\")\n",
        "print(template_explanation)\n"
      ]
    },
    {
      "cell_type": "markdown",
      "id": "41190fa1",
      "metadata": {
        "id": "41190fa1"
      },
      "source": [
        "\n",
        "**Benefits of a Generative AI explanation layer:**\n",
        "\n",
        "* **Natural-language accessibility** — SHAP/LIME output (numeric contributions, feature-threshold rules) is precise but not naturally readable by most end users; an LLM can translate it into fluent, personalised prose, as approximated above.\n",
        "* **Conversational interaction** — users could probe *\"why not X?\"* or *\"show me something cheaper but similar\"*, something static SHAP/LIME plots cannot support.\n",
        "* **Potential for richer context** — an LLM could weave in product descriptions, review themes, or seasonal context alongside the numeric feature drivers.\n",
        "\n",
        "**Risks:**\n",
        "\n",
        "* **Hallucination** — an LLM generating free-text explanations may invent plausible-sounding but false reasons (e.g. claiming a product is \"eco-friendly\" when it is not, or fabricating a customer's stated preference), which is especially dangerous when the explanation is expected to be *faithful* to the model's actual reasoning, not merely fluent.\n",
        "* **Bias amplification** — since our own analysis (§18) shows the underlying model favours popular items, an LLM asked to justify these recommendations could produce persuasive-sounding rationalisations for an already-biased system, making the bias *harder to notice* rather than easier, because the explanation reads as authoritative and well-reasoned.\n",
        "* **Misleading / unfaithful explanations** — a known risk in XAI research generally: a generated explanation can *sound* plausible without accurately reflecting the true computational basis of the recommendation (the gap between SHAP's mathematically-grounded attribution and an LLM's paraphrase of it is a genuine faithfulness risk).\n",
        "* **Privacy** — feeding customer-level features (spend, purchase history, country) into a prompt increases the surface area for sensitive data exposure, especially if a third-party hosted LLM API is used.\n",
        "* **User manipulation** — persuasive natural language is inherently more capable of nudging behaviour than a bar chart; a badly-incentivised deployment could use LLM-generated explanations to *justify* upselling or dark-pattern-style recommendations rather than to inform.\n",
        "* **Over-reliance / automation bias** — fluent, confident-sounding explanations can lead users (and even internal reviewers/auditors) to trust the system's outputs more than the underlying evidence warrants, reducing critical scrutiny exactly where it is most needed.\n",
        "* **Accountability** — if an LLM-generated explanation is later found to be inaccurate or misleading, responsibility is harder to assign across the recommendation model, the explanation-generation model, and the deploying organisation, complicating governance and redress.\n",
        "\n",
        "**Does Generative AI help or complicate the popularity-bias issue identified in Part 2?** It is genuinely double-edged. On one hand, a GenAI layer could **help**: it could be explicitly prompted/constrained to disclose when a recommendation is popularity-driven (\"this is one of our most popular items — here's a less common alternative you might also like\"), turning the SHAP/LIME evidence of popularity-bias into a transparency feature rather than a hidden defect, and could support the long-tail mitigation of Section 20 by generating persuasive, well-explained descriptions specifically for *promoted long-tail items*, helping them compete for user attention against popular items on quality of explanation rather than sheer purchase volume alone. On the other hand, it could **complicate** the issue: an LLM optimised purely for engaging, fluent copy has no inherent incentive to surface unfavourable truths like \"this recommendation exists mainly because it's popular, not because it's a great match for you\" — without deliberate design and evaluation for **faithfulness** (not just fluency), a generative explanation layer risks becoming a more persuasive way to *disguise* the very bias this notebook set out to detect and mitigate.\n"
      ]
    },

      "source": [
        "\n",
        "## 23. Overall Discussion\n",
        "\n",
        "RetailRecX demonstrates a coherent pipeline connecting **predictive performance**, **explainability**, and **ethics**, rather than treating them as separate add-ons:\n",
        "\n",
        "* The underlying **recommendation model** (Section 11) achieves strong discrimination (validation ROC-AUC) and produces genuinely personalised top-K lists (Section 12), evaluated honestly via a leakage-aware temporal split (Section 10) against real held-out purchases (Section 13).\n",
        "* **XAI (SHAP + LIME, Sections 15–17)** did not just satisfy a reporting requirement — it *directly surfaced* the mechanism behind the ethical problem investigated next: both methods repeatedly highlighted product-popularity features as major score drivers for individual recommendations, which motivated and was confirmed by the dedicated popularity-bias analysis.\n",
        "* **Ethics and mitigation (Sections 18–21)** showed the bias is not just theoretically plausible but empirically measurable, and that it *can* be reduced through two structurally different, complementary interventions, each with a distinct, quantified accuracy/fairness trade-off — there is no single \"correct\" answer, only an explicit, evidence-based choice of operating point.\n",
        "* **Generative AI (Section 22)** was assessed not as a generic \"add an LLM\" feature, but specifically in terms of how it would interact with the *exact* ethical issue already demonstrated in this system — showing it can be designed to either expose or obscure the very popularity bias uncovered above, depending on how faithfully it is built and evaluated.\n",
        "\n",
        "The overarching lesson is that transparency (XAI) and fairness (bias mitigation) are not independent boxes to tick: in RetailRecX, the SHAP/LIME explanations were the evidence base that made the ethical issue *demonstrable* rather than merely asserted, and the same feature-attribution machinery could, in principle, be reused to *monitor* whether future mitigation strategies (or a future GenAI explanation layer) are working as intended.\n"
      ]
    },

        "\n",
        "## 24. Limitations\n",
        "\n",
        "* **Dataset age and scope.** The Online Retail dataset covers December 2010–December 2011 for a single UK-based gift wholesaler; customer behaviour, product catalogues, and popularity dynamics in modern, larger-scale e-commerce platforms may differ substantially.\n",
        "* **Sparse interactions.** Most customer–product pairs are never observed; the negative-sampling approach used to build a supervised training set (Section 11) is a common but imperfect approximation of \"true disinterest\" — many sampled negatives may in fact be latent positives the customer simply never encountered.\n",
        "* **No demographic information.** Beyond `Country`, no customer demographic or explicit preference data is available, limiting both personalisation richness and the ability to analyse *demographic* fairness (as distinct from the popularity/item-side fairness studied here).\n",
        "* **Cold-start problem.** New customers or new products with no training-period history cannot be scored by RetailRecX in its current form (Section 10) — a common limitation of interaction-history-based recommenders, typically addressed with content-based or hybrid fallback strategies not implemented here.\n",
        "* **Limited product semantics.** Only `Description` text is available for products; no structured category/taxonomy data exists, which constrains feature richness (e.g. no true \"category popularity\" or content-based similarity feature) and constrains explanation quality (SHAP/LIME can reference `StockCode`-level popularity but not richer semantic properties).\n",
        "* **Offline evaluation only.** Precision@K/Recall@K/NDCG@K/Hit Rate are standard but imperfect proxies for real user satisfaction; they cannot capture, e.g., whether a \"correct\" recommendation was actually noticed, clicked, or valued by the customer, nor longer-term effects like trust or retention.\n",
        "* **Potential residual bias beyond popularity.** This notebook focuses specifically on popularity bias; other ethically relevant issues (e.g. country/regional bias in `cust_country_enc`, price-sensitivity-driven exclusion of premium or budget shoppers) were not exhaustively investigated and may also be present.\n",
        "* **Mitigation operating points are illustrative, not optimised.** The α and quota values selected in Sections 19–20 were chosen to clearly illustrate the trade-off curve, not tuned against a formal fairness-accuracy objective function or real business KPIs.\n"
      ]
    },

        "\n",
        "## 25. Conclusion\n",
        "\n",
        "This notebook built RetailRecX, a personalised e-commerce recommender trained on the real Online Retail transaction dataset, and used it as a live case study for the three parts of this assignment. A Random-Forest-based customer–product scoring model was trained under a leakage-aware temporal split and evaluated with standard top-K recommendation metrics against genuine held-out purchases. **SHAP** and **LIME** were both applied to real trained-model outputs (not illustrative toy examples) and directly compared on the same recommendation instance, satisfying Part 1's requirement for two distinct, compared XAI methods. This XAI analysis motivated an empirical investigation of **popularity bias**, which was clearly demonstrated using real recommendation-slot statistics, explained mechanistically, and assessed for its impact on users, sellers, diversity, fairness, and autonomy. Two structurally different mitigation strategies — popularity-aware re-ranking and long-tail quota re-ranking — were implemented and evaluated before/after, revealing genuine, quantified accuracy-vs-fairness trade-offs, satisfying Part 2. Finally, the potential integration of **Generative AI** as a natural-language explanation layer was critically examined specifically in relation to the popularity-bias issue already demonstrated, concluding that its effect is double-edged and depends heavily on whether it is designed and evaluated for *faithfulness* to the underlying model, not just fluency — satisfying Part 3. Overall, RetailRecX shows that explainability and ethical auditing are most powerful when treated as a connected pipeline — where XAI evidence directly informs and substantiates ethical claims, rather than being produced in isolation.\n"
      ]
